title: Hotel Reservations
prompt: Design the booking system for a hotel group: guests search for a room type over a date range, book it, and can cancel later.

clarify.q: Do guests book a specific room number or a room type ("Deluxe King")?
clarify.why: Booking by type means we only track a count per type per night and assign room numbers at check-in. Specific rooms would turn this into a seat-map problem.

clarify.q: Is overbooking allowed, and by how much?
clarify.why: Hotels often sell slightly above capacity because some guests cancel or do not show. The limit becomes part of the inventory check rather than a hard total.

clarify.q: Do guests pay at booking, or pay at the hotel?
clarify.why: Paying up front adds a payment step that can fail after inventory is taken, so we need a pending state and a compensation path.

clarify.q: How many hotels and rooms, and how far ahead can people book?
clarify.why: Hotels × room types × days ahead is the size of the inventory table. It tells us whether one database is enough.
Free cancellation until a deadline, then a fee, means cancellations are a write path with money attached, not just a delete.

clarify.q: Do outside sites (travel agencies) sell our rooms too?
clarify.why: Other channels make inventory a shared resource with external writers. That needs a channel sync and makes overselling more likely.

functional: Search a hotel or city for available room types and prices over check-in and check-out dates.
Book N rooms of a type for a date range; the booking succeeds for every night or for none.
Retrying a booking request never creates a second reservation.
Cancel a reservation, applying the hotel's fee rules and returning the inventory.
Hotel staff can change room counts, prices and the overbooking limit per room type and date.
nonFunctional: Never sell more than the configured limit (capacity plus overbooking allowance) for any room type and night.
Search p99 under 500 ms; prices and availability may be up to 1 minute stale in search.
Booking p99 under 1 s, excluding the payment provider's own time.
99.9% availability for booking; search can degrade to cached results.
Reservations are durable once confirmed: no loss after a single node failure.
outOfScope: Loyalty points and member pricing rules.
Housekeeping and room-number assignment at check-in.

assumptions: 5,000 hotels, 200 rooms each on average = 1 M rooms
10 room types per hotel; bookable up to 365 days ahead
A reservation record is about 1 KB

steps.label: Inventory rows
steps.result: ≈ 18 M rows × ~50 B ≈ 0.9 GB. Fits in RAM on one database.

steps.label: Reservations per day
steps.math: 1 M rooms × 70% = 700 k room-nights/night; 700 k / 2.5 nights per stay = 280 k bookings/day

steps.label: Booking writes per second
steps.result: ≈ 3/s average, ~30/s peak. Each touches ~2.5 inventory rows.

steps.label: Reservation storage
steps.result: ≈ 100 GB/year: one Postgres with yearly partitions

estimates.takeaway: Writes are tiny (about 30/s at peak) and the whole inventory is under 1 GB, so a single Postgres primary with a synchronous replica can own all booking state with real transactions. No sharding needed. Search is 100× the volume, so it reads from replicas and a cache that may be up to a minute stale, while the booking transaction always checks the primary.

api.note: Served from replicas plus a short cache. 'available' is a hint, not a promise.

api.body: { hotelId, roomTypeId, checkIn, checkOut, rooms, guest, paymentToken? }
api.note: Idempotency-Key header is required. The client creates it when the booking form loads.
Idempotent: cancelling twice returns the same result.

api.body: { roomTypeId, from, to, totalRooms?, overbookPct?, price? }
api.note: Staff only. Lowering totalRooms below current bookings is rejected, not silently applied.

entities.name: RoomTypeInventory
entities.why: One row per room type per night. Booking is a conditional increment of 'reserved' across the nights of the stay.

entities.name: Reservation
fields: detects key reuse with a different body
entities.why: The guest's booking. The unique idempotency key is what makes retries safe.

entities.name: OutboxEvent
entities.why: Emails, channel sync and search cache updates are sent from here, so they are never lost and never sent for a rolled-back booking.

data.note: The key access pattern is "rows for one room type, consecutive nights", which the primary key (hotelId, roomTypeId, night) serves with a single range scan. A CHECK (reserved <= totalRooms * (100 + overbookPct) / 100) constraint is a last line of defence even if application code has a bug. Search uses read replicas. If the group grew to hundreds of thousands of hotels, hotelId is the natural shard key, since a booking never spans two hotels.

hld.summary:
Guests reach a search service that reads from Postgres replicas and a Redis cache of availability per hotel and month. It can be a minute stale because it only suggests options. The reservation service owns writes: it checks the idempotency key, runs the inventory transaction on the primary, and records an outbox event in the same transaction.

If payment is taken up front, the reservation starts as pending with a 10-minute expiry, and becomes confirmed once the payment provider answers. A relay reads the outbox and publishes events to a queue, which drives confirmation emails, cache invalidation and sync to outside sales channels.

diagram.title: Search reads replicas, booking writes the primary
diagram.src:

  GW --> S[Search service]

  S --> RR[("Postgres replicas")]

flows.title: Booking 2 Deluxe rooms for 3 nights
steps: Client sends POST with the Idempotency-Key created when the form opened.
Service inserts the reservation row as pending; if the key already exists with the same request hash, it returns the stored result instead.
In the same transaction it increments reserved by 2 on the 3 inventory rows, only where reserved + 2 is within the limit.
If fewer than 3 rows changed, it rolls back and returns 409 sold out.
On commit, it charges the card; success marks the reservation confirmed and writes an outbox event.

flows.title: Cancelling
steps: Guest calls cancel; the service locks the reservation row and checks status is confirmed.
It computes the fee from the deadline, decrements reserved on each night, sets status cancelled and writes an outbox event, all in one transaction.
A worker issues the refund through the provider with the reservation id as its idempotency key.

flows.title: A pending booking whose payment never finishes
steps: The guest closes the app after the inventory step.
A sweeper every minute finds pending reservations older than 10 minutes.
It asks the payment provider for status by idempotency key; if not paid, it marks the reservation expired and returns inventory in one transaction.

deepDives.title: Modelling inventory
deepDives.problem: We need to answer "are 2 Deluxe rooms free on each of 12, 13 and 14 March?" quickly and update it safely. The naive model, one row per physical room with a list of bookings, makes every check a search for overlapping date ranges.

options.name: Per physical room, check overlaps
options.how: Store reservations with a room number and search for any booking whose range overlaps the request.
pros: Room assignment is done at booking time
Matches how a small guesthouse thinks
cons: Overlap queries are hard to lock correctly (you lock rows that do not exist yet)
Forces picking a room number months ahead

options.name: Count per room type per night
options.how: One row per hotel, room type and night with totalRooms and reserved. A booking increments reserved on each night.
pros: Check and update are a simple range of rows
Overbooking is just a higher limit
cons: Room numbers are assigned later, at check-in
Changing a room's type means editing counts, not just a label

deepDives.choice: Use counts per room type per night. Guests book a type, the hotel assigns the number on arrival, and the count model makes concurrency simple. I would only track physical rooms at booking time if the product sold specific rooms ("room 1204 with the sea view"), and then I would model those as their own room type of size 1.

deepDives.title: Two guests, one last room
deepDives.problem: Two requests for the last Deluxe room on 13 March arrive together. Both read reserved = 49 of 50 and both think they can book. With a multi-night stay, the transaction must also succeed on every night or on none.

options.name: Read, then lock and write
options.how: SELECT the nights FOR UPDATE in date order, check limits in code, UPDATE, COMMIT.
pros: Any rule can be checked in code
cons: Two round trips while holding locks
Must always lock in date order to avoid deadlocks

options.name: Single conditional update
options.how: UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + $n WHERE hotelId=$h AND roomTypeId=$t AND night >= $in AND night < $out AND reserved + $n <= totalRooms * (100 + overbookPct) / 100; commit only if rows changed = number of nights.
pros: One statement, locks held for microseconds
The database serialises the two writers on the row
cons: The rule must fit in SQL
Row-count check is easy to forget in code review

options.name: Version column (optimistic)
options.how: Read rows with a version; UPDATE ... WHERE version = $v; retry on mismatch.
pros: No locks held between read and write
cons: Retries pile up for popular hotels and dates
More code than the conditional update for the same result

deepDives.choice: Use the single conditional update inside the same transaction that inserts the reservation. At 30 writes/s the lock time does not matter, and the row-count check gives all-or-nothing across nights. Postgres's default isolation is enough here because the update re-checks the condition on the latest row version. I would switch to read-then-lock only if rules grew beyond one expression, such as minimum-stay rules that depend on other nights.

diagram.title: The last room on one night
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Guest A
  participant B as Guest B
  participant R as Reservation service
  participant D as Postgres
  A->>R: book 1 room, 12 to 15 March
  B->>R: book 1 room, 13 to 14 March
  R->>D: conditional update for A, 3 nights
  D-->>R: 3 rows changed, commit
  R-->>A: 201 pending
  R->>D: conditional update for B, 1 night
  D-->>R: 0 rows changed, roll back
  R-->>B: 409 sold out

deepDives.title: Idempotent bookings
deepDives.problem: A guest taps Book, the network drops, the app retries. Without care we either create two reservations and charge twice, or tell the guest it failed when it worked.

options.name: Client-generated idempotency key
options.how: App creates a UUID when the form loads and sends it on every retry. The reservation table has a unique index on (guestId, idempotencyKey) and stores the response.
pros: Works across app restarts if the key is saved
cons: Needs a request hash to catch a reused key with different dates
Keys must be kept as long as retries can arrive, say 24 hours

options.name: Deduplicate on content
options.how: Treat same guest, hotel and dates within 5 minutes as a duplicate.
cons: Blocks a guest who really wants two separate bookings
The time window is a guess

deepDives.choice: Use the client-generated key, stored in the same transaction as the reservation so a key can never exist without its result. A retry with the same key and same body returns the stored response; a different body returns 422. The same reservation id is then passed to the payment provider as its idempotency key, so the charge is also safe to retry. Content-based dedup is only a fallback for old clients that do not send keys.

deepDives.title: Payment, pending holds and cancellation
deepDives.problem: Inventory and payment live in different systems, so they cannot share one transaction. If we take inventory and payment then fails, or the app vanishes mid-payment, rooms stay locked for nobody.

options.name: Charge first, then book
options.how: Charge the card, then try the inventory update; refund if sold out.
pros: Never hold inventory for an unpaid guest
cons: Charging and refunding a guest who got nothing looks bad on their statement
Refund delays are days, not seconds

options.name: Book pending, then charge (saga)
options.how: Take inventory with status pending and a 10-minute expiry, charge, then confirm; on failure or expiry, release inventory.
pros: Guests are only charged for rooms they have
Each step has a clear compensating step
cons: Rooms are briefly held by people who will not pay
Needs a sweeper and a provider status check

deepDives.choice: Use book pending, then charge. A 10-minute hold on a 50-room type barely dents availability. The sweeper asks the provider before expiring a booking, because a slow success must not be thrown away. Cancellation reverses the same steps: release inventory and record the fee in one transaction, then refund through an outbox-driven worker. If most hotels used pay-at-hotel, I would skip the pending state for them and confirm immediately.

failures: Promote the synchronous replica; idempotency keys make client retries safe; search keeps working from cache and other replicas.
Payment provider times out after charging
Reservation stays pending; the sweeper queries the provider by reservation id and confirms instead of expiring.
Search cache shows a room that is sold out
The booking transaction is the only truth and returns 409 with alternatives; cache entries for that hotel are invalidated from the outbox event.
Outside channel sells the same last room at the same time
Give each channel an allotment of rooms, or accept a small overbooking within the configured limit; sync changes within seconds through the event queue.
Bookings still commit; emails and channel sync are delayed, not lost; alert when the oldest unsent event is over 2 minutes old.
scale: 10× hotels (50,000): 180 M inventory rows, about 9 GB, and ~300 writes/s at peak; still one primary, maybe a larger instance.
100× (an online travel agency): shard by hotelId; a booking never spans hotels, so no cross-shard transactions; search moves to a dedicated index rebuilt from events.
Holiday peak on a few hotels: hot rows are per hotel and night, and only a handful of writers compete; conditional updates keep lock time tiny, so it still holds.

followups.q: How do you support a guest changing their dates?
answer: Treat it as one transaction: release the old nights and reserve the new nights together.
If the new nights are sold out, roll back and keep the original booking.
Recompute the price and charge or refund the difference afterwards.
Limit is totalRooms plus a per-night percentage, say 5%.
Hotel staff see when reserved exceeds physical rooms and plan walk-outs (rebooking a guest at a partner hotel).
Turn the allowance down close to the date when no-show risk is lower.

followups.q: How fresh does the search cache need to be?
answer: A minute is fine for hotels with plenty of rooms.
When a room type falls below 3 available for a night, skip the cache for it, so guests see sold-out states quickly.
Invalidate from outbox events, with a 60 s TTL as the backstop.

followups.q: What if an admin lowers the room count after rooms are sold?
answer: Reject changes that put totalRooms below reserved for any night and show which nights conflict.
Allow it only with an explicit override that marks bookings for manual relocation.

mistakes: Modelling inventory as physical rooms and searching date overlaps, then struggling to lock it.
Checking availability with a SELECT and then booking with a separate UPDATE, with no condition on the write.
Reaching for sharding or NoSQL when the numbers say 30 writes/s and 1 GB of inventory.
Charging the card without an idempotency key, so a retry double-charges.
Trusting the cached search result as the final availability.

mid: Asked whether guests book a room type or a specific room
Modelled inventory as one row per room type per night
Made the booking all-or-nothing across nights with a transaction
Required an idempotency key on POST /reservations and explained what it stores
Separated search (stale is fine) from booking (always the primary)
senior: Used a conditional update with a row-count check and explained why it prevents oversell
Handled overbooking as a configurable limit in the same check
Designed the pending state, expiry sweeper and provider status check
Used an outbox so emails and channel sync never fire for rolled-back bookings
staff: Discussed external channels sharing inventory and how to split allotments
Named hotelId as the shard key and why no booking crosses shards
Proposed adaptive cache bypass when availability gets low
